chunks: "A via is a small plated hole through the board that connects copper on one layer to copper on another.
The fab drills the hole, then plates copper onto the wall, so the wall becomes a tiny copper tube, called the barrel, that joins pads on the layers it passes through.
We need them because a multilayer board is a 3-D structure and traces can only run in 2-D on each layer.
When two traces would have to cross, or when a chip pin on the top has to get to a ground plane on layer two, or a power rail has to reach a pin from an inner plane, the signal drops through a via.
They also carry heat from a hot component to a copper plane on the other side. The thing I'd add is that a via isn't a perfect wire. A standard 0. 3 mm via through a 1.
6 mm board is about a milliohm of resistance, but around 1 nanohenries of inductance and a few tenths of a picofarad of capacitance. At low frequency you ignore it.
At a gigahertz that inductance is several ohms, and you have to think about it. That's why high-speed designers count vias and put a ground via next to every signal via."
